en: In addition, when running Py, there also is
a
--tools
flag you can add.
Now, what does this do? It allows you to add
a comma-separated list of the tools you
wanna give Py when it starts. Now, by
default, Py has all its built-in tools,
which is just a few, and then all the tools
any extensions or packages may have added,
but we'll get back to extensions and
packages later. So here, for example, I
could give Pi access to the find, read, ls,
and grep tools,
which are 4 of the tools that are built into
Pi.
And the official docs list all the tools
that are built in.
And now the Pi session would start with only
those tools enabled.
And for example,
the edit, write, or bash tools would not be
provided. So it would actually not be able
to write any files. It can just read files
with these tools, find and read files.
Why would you do that? Well, if you were
starting a session where you want Py to
review
your code, for example, and you wanna make
sure that it doesn't edit anything yet or
delete anything,
you could be extra safe and sure that it
can't do that by just giving it read tools.
And now there is no way for Py to
circumvent that or write a script because it
can't write anything. It can just read. So
that could be very useful for research or
review tasks where you don't want it to mess
up things.
You also have the
exclude-tools
flag, which is just the opposite. There you
could exclude certain tools and for example,
exclude bash, write, and edit. And now
again, it starts a session and certain tools
are disabled now.
So either way, you have some controls over
which tools are available and loaded by Py.
You can also use the no-tools flag if you
wanna start it totally without any tools to
basically use it like an old-school chatbot,
which only has its internal knowledge base,
so to say.
This is probably not too useful like this,
but it can be useful if you, for example,
have a file with some content in it and you
want Pi to summarize it. And here I'll just
use that output text file, which I had Pi
create before, but of course,
You can use any file.
You could pipe that into py
-p
--notools
and say summarize this content.
And it can now do that because you pass that
as extra input to it. That is possible. You
can pipe input into py and have it summarize
this and give it no tools to make sure it
can't read anything or write anything else.
A bit niche, but interesting to know, which
is why I wanted to show it here.
There also is py
--nobuiltintools
so that all those built-in tools would be
disabled. But if you had installed extra
packages that add new tools, again,
something we'll get back to later,
those would still be available. So a
variation of --notools that does not disable
all tools, but just the built-in tools.
Again, not something I'm using all the time,
to be very honest, but something that can be
useful for specific tasks, especially if
you're building maybe your own scripts on
top of Pi that call Pi for summarizing
articles or anything like that. Disabling
tools could then be an interesting option.
